core: What management is: getting work done through others, efficiently (working definition attributed to OpenStax Introduction to Business 6.1)
What leadership is: influencing and inspiring others toward a goal (working definition attributed to OpenStax Principles of Management 13.1, corroborated by Introduction to Business 6.4)
The contrast: manager plans, organizes, controls (position, appointment, compliance) versus leader provides vision, inspiration, influence (follower acceptance, intrinsic commitment)
The overlap: good managers lead; good leaders manage
The four functions previewed: planning, organizing, leading, controlling, each named with one line
Both matter: organizations need management and leadership, with an original example
The honest framing: two hats, often one head
supporting: Managers' daily work is conversational and fragmented (Mintzberg/Kotter studies in OpenStax POM 1.1)
Leadership is a process built over time between leader and follower (POM 13.2)
outOfScope: Planning, organizing, leading, controlling as full topics (each has its own sibling lesson)
Leadership styles (autocratic, participative, free rein) — sibling topic leadership-styles
Sources and bases of power in depth — sibling topic power-and-influence

claims.claim: Management is the process of guiding the development, maintenance, and allocation of resources to attain organizational goals; in plain words, getting work done through others, efficiently.
Efficiency means using the least possible amount of resources to get work done, while effectiveness means producing a desired result; managers need both to achieve organizational goals.
The management process rests on four functions — planning, organizing, leading, and controlling — which form a tightly integrated cycle rather than separate boxes.

Leadership is defined by OpenStax's Principles of Management as a social (interpersonal) influence relationship between two or more persons who depend on each other to attain certain mutual goals in a group situation; in plain words, influencing and inspiring others toward a goal.

A leader can be anyone in an organization, regardless of position, able to influence others to act or follow, often by their own choice; organizations need effective leadership at all levels to meet goals and remain competitive.

Managers and leaders differ in how they come to their roles and where their influence comes from: managers are generally appointed and exercise rights that come with their position, while leaders emerge from followers' acceptance and draw power from expertise, personality, and the working relationship; followers of a leader comply because they want to.

The two concepts are not interchangeable, nor are they redundant; good management often requires leadership, and effective leadership often calls for the ability to manage — to set goals, plan, implement strategy, solve problems, and organize and control.
Managers often succeed or fail because of their ability or inability to lead.
Leadership is a process — a complex, dynamic exchange relationship built over time between leader and follower — and the follower is the most critical factor in any leadership event.
Real managerial work is fragmented and conversational: studies found managers switch tasks constantly and spend most of their working time with other people, in short interactions.
Warren Bennis observed that many organizations are overmanaged and underled, and John Kotter argued there is a leadership crisis; leadership is an urgently needed quality in all managerial roles.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the contrast between management and leadership sharp or blurred?
positions: Some popular frameworks present management and leadership as near-opposites (managers cope with complexity, leaders with change)
OpenStax's Principles of Management 13.1 says the two concepts are not interchangeable nor redundant, yet also says good management requires leadership and effective leadership requires managing
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the distinction first (different definitions, different sources of influence) and then the overlap as the honest reality: two hats, often one head. It never claims the roles are opposites or that one outranks the other.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which list of management functions should the lesson use?
positions: Introduction to Business 6.1 lists planning, organizing, leading, and controlling
Principles of Management 13.1, citing its companion text, lists planning, organizing, directing, and controlling
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses planning, organizing, leading, and controlling (Introduction to Business 6.1) because those four are the subject's sibling topics and match the curriculum queue.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's boilerplate (e.g., 'Management Versus Leadership is a foundational concept in Management & Leadership. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it') asserts nothing verifiable and was discarded.

The draft's claim that the topic 'is a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' in college courses was not tied to any source and was replaced with documented value from the research.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic boilerplate with source-verified definitions and attributed working definitions.
Working definitions now attributed: management to OpenStax's Introduction to Business 6.1; leadership to OpenStax's Principles of Management 13.1 with corroboration from Introduction to Business 6.4.
All examples replaced with original scenarios (City Light Bikes, Nadia's restaurant, the food drive, the clinic office manager, the nurse, the line cook, the moving company).
